latin: duos tamen deos et duos dominos nunquam ex ore nostro proferimus: non quasi non et pater deus et filius deus et spiritus sanctus deus, et deus unusquisque, sed quoniam retro et duo dii et duo domini praedicabantur, ut, ubi venisset Christus, et deus agnosceretur et dominus vocaretur quia filius dei et domini.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 18 = PDF p. 48 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-048.png. Kroymann 1907 p.18 reads 'numquam' (LL 'nunquam'), 'spiritus deus et dominus unusquisque' (LL 'spiritus sanctus deus, et deus unusquisque'), '<ideo> retro' (LL 'quoniam retro'), 'uenisset' (LL 'venisset'). ANF's 'each is God' follows the LL reading, not Kroymann's.
english: That there are, however, two Gods or two Lords, is a statement which at no time proceeds out of our mouth: not as if it were untrue that the Father is God, and the Son is God, and the Holy Ghost is God, and each is God; but because in earlier times Two were actually spoken of as God, and two as Lord, that when Christ should come He might be both acknowledged as God and designated as Lord, being the Son of Him who is both God and Lord.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 608 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian denies that he ever says 'two Gods' or 'two Lords' as a statement, while affirming that Father, Son and Spirit are each God.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (answer to the charge of two Gods)
limits: He concedes that earlier Scripture spoke of 'two Gods' and 'two Lords' (ch. 13.1-4), and the objection is built on that concession. The phrase 'each is God' is ANF's rendering of 'deus unusquisque'. Kroymann 1907 p. 18 reads 'numquam' and 'spiritus deus et dominus unusquisque' ('each is Lord'), so the ANF follows a different text at that point.

latin: Thronus tuus, deus, in aevum, <virga directionis> virga regni tui; dilexisti iustitiam et odisti iniquitatem, propterea� unxit te deus, deus tuus. si ad deum loquitur, et unctum deum a deo, affirmat et hic duos deos +pro virga regni tui+.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 17 = PDF p. 47 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-047.png. The Latin also has an unreadable character after 'propterea' in LL and the line 'propterea� unxit'.
english: Now, since He here speaks to God, and affirms that God is anointed by God, He must have affirmed that Two are God, by reason of the sceptre's royal power.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 607 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)

what_it_says: Tertullian reads Psalm 44 (LXX; 45 in Hebrew numbering) as addressing God and calling God 'anointed by God', and so as naming two beings who are God.
use: objection (Arian-type reading: God anointed by God); the answer is in ch. 13.3-9
limits: This is the hardest text in the chapter; the Latin has crux-marks (+...+) that Kroymann brackets as '[pro uirga regni tui]'. Psalm 45:6-7 is the usual reference for this objection.

latin: In principio erat sermo et sermo erat apud deum et deus erat sermo: unus qui erat, et alius penes quem erat.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. John 1:1 There was One who was, and there was another with whom He was.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 607 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian quotes John 1:1 as naming one who was and another with whom He was, and so as showing two persons.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (John 1:1 as two persons)
limits: The 'alius' here is the first use of the 'other' language that Tertullian explains in ch. 21 (item 17). Opponents read the two as two separate beings; he answers this in ch. 13.5-9.

latin: ut si homines per fidem filios dei factos� deos scriptura pronuntiare non timuit, scias illam multo magis vero et unico dei filio <dei> et domini nomen iure contulisse.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: in order that, if the Scripture has not been afraid to designate as gods human beings, who have become sons of God by faith, you may be sure that the same Scripture has with greater propriety conferred the name of the Lord on the true and one only Son of God.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 608 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian argues that Scripture calls men 'gods' (Psalm 82) so the Son can more properly be called Lord.
use: answer to objection (Psalm 82: 'gods' applied to men)
limits: This is an argument from usage (the Son is called Lord more properly than men are called gods). It does not explain how the Son is God in the same substance as the Father.

latin: nos enim, qui et tempora et causas, scripturarum per dei gratiam inspicimus, maxime paracleti non hominum discipuli, duos quidem definimus, patrem et filium, et iam tres cum spiritu sancto, secundum rationem oeconomiae quae facit numerum, ne, ut vestra perversitas infert, pater ipse credatur natus et passus, quod non licet credi quoniam non ita traditum est.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: For we, who by the grace of God possess an insight into both the times and the occasions of the Sacred Writings, especially we who are followers of the Paraclete, not of human teachers, do indeed definitively declare that Two Beings are God, the Father and the Son, and, with the addition of the Holy Spirit, even Three, according to the principle of the divine economy, which introduces number, in order that the Father may not, as you perversely infer, be Himself believed to have been born and to have suffered, which it is not lawful to believe, forasmuch as it has not been so handed down.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 608 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Church defines two, Father and Son, and three with the Spirit, according to the economy, and that the Father must not be said to be born or to suffer.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (three in the economy); answer to the claim that the Father suffered
limits: 'Three' is an economic number (secundum rationem oeconomiae), and it is used to protect the Father from suffering; it is not yet the Nicene formula of three persons in one substance.

latin: ceterum si ex conscientia qua scimus dei nomen et domini et patri et filio et spiritui convenire deos et dominos nominaremus, extinxissemus faces nostras
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: Besides, if, from that perfect knowledge which assures us that the title of God and Lord is suitable both to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Ghost, we were to invoke a plurality of gods and lords, we should quench our torches
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 608 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the title 'God and Lord' suits the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and that Christians should not swear by a plurality of gods and lords.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (God and Lord title shared by Father, Son and Spirit)
limits: This is a pastoral argument about martyrdom and idolatry, not a dogmatic definition.

latin: itaque deos omnino non dicam nec dominos, sed apostolum sequar ut si pariter nominandi fuerint pater et filius deum patrem appellem et Iesum Christum dominum nominem. solum autem Christum potero deum dicere, sicut idem apostolus: Ex quibus Christus, qui est, inquit, deus super omnia, benedictus in aevum omne.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 19 = PDF p. 49 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-049.png. Kroymann 1907 p.19 reads 'solum autem Christum potero deum dicere' (same).
english: I will therefore not speak of gods at all, nor of lords, but I shall follow the apostle; so that if the Father and the Son, are alike to be invoked, I shall call the Father God, and invoke Jesus Christ as Lord. Romans 1:7 But when Christ alone (is mentioned), I shall be able to call Him God, as the same apostle says: Of whom is Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever. Romans 9:5
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 608 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian will call the Father God and Christ Lord when both are named, but calls Christ alone God, citing Romans 9:5.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Christ alone called God, Rom. 9:5); this is the answer to the brief's 'Deum ... dicimus' question
limits: The phrase 'Deum ... dicimus' does not occur in ch. 13-25 (negative search of the Latin Library text). The nearest is 'solum autem Christum potero deum dicere' (ch. 13.9), quoted here.

latin: nam et radium solis seorsum solem vocabo: solem autem nominans cuius est radius, non statim et radium solem appellabo. nam etsi soles duos faciam, tamen et solem et radium eius tam duas res et duas species unius et indivisae substantiae numerabo quam deum et sermonem eius, quam patrem et filium.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 19 = PDF p. 49 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-049.png. Kroymann 1907 p.19 reads 'nam nec soles duos faciam' where LL reads 'nam etsi soles duos faciam'; ANF 'although I make not two suns' follows the LL reading. 'unius et indiuisae substantiae' is the same in both.
english: For I should give the name of sun even to a sunbeam, considered in itself; but if I were mentioning the sun from which the ray emanates, I certainly should at once withdraw the name of sun from the mere beam. For although I make not two suns, still I shall reckon both the sun and its ray to be as much two things and two forms of one undivided substance, as God and His Word, as the Father and the Son.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 608 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the sun and its ray are two forms of one undivided substance, and so God and His Word, the Father and the Son, are two forms of one undivided substance.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (one undivided substance, two forms)
limits: The sun-and-ray image makes the Son a derived form of the Father; opponents read the image as subordination. Tertullian says 'one undivided substance', not 'consubstantial'.

latin: iam ergo alius erit qui videbatur, quia non potest idem invisibilis definiri qui videbatur: et consequens erit ut invisibilem patrem intellegamus pro plenitudine maiestatis, visibilem vero filium agnoscamus pro modulo derivationis, sicut nec solem nobis contemplari licet quantum ad ipsam substantiae summam quae est in caelis, radium autem eius toleramus oculis pro temperatura portionis quae in terram inde porrigitur.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 20 = PDF p. 50 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-050.png. Kroymann 1907 p.20 agrees ('pro modulo deriuationis', 'radium autem eius toleramus oculis').
english: Now, then, He must be a different Being who was seen, because of one who was seen it could not be predicated that He is invisible. It will therefore follow, that by Him who is invisible we must understand the Father in the fullness of His majesty, while we recognise the Son as visible by reason of the dispensation of His derived existence; even as it is not permitted us to contemplate the sun, in the full amount of his substance which is in the heavens, but we can only endure with our eyes a ray, by reason of the tempered condition of this portion which is projected from him to the earth.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 609 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Father is invisible in the fullness of His majesty and the Son is visible by reason of His derived existence, as we can endure a ray of the sun but not look at the sun itself.
use: answer to objection (Father invisible, Son visible: Ex. 33:20; Moses)
limits: The 'ray' image makes the visible Son a derived portion of the Father; this is the same image as in item 8. Kroymann 1907 p.20 has 'pro modulo deriuationis' (same words).

latin: et filium suo nomine eatenus invisibilem, qua sermo et spiritus dei, ex substantiae condicione iam nunc, [et qua deus et sermo et spiritus dei] visibilem autem fuisse ante carnem eo modo quo dicit ad Aaron et Mariam,
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 21 = PDF p. 51 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-051.png. Kroymann 1907 p.21 reads 'ex substantiae condicione, [iam nunc et quia deus et sermo et spiritus dei,] uisibilem' (LL: 'ex substantiae condicione iam nunc, [et qua deus et sermo et spiritus dei] visibilem'); 'quia' vs 'qua'.
english: We declare, however, that the Son also, considered in Himself (as the Son), is invisible, in that He is God, and the Word and Spirit of God; but that He was visible before the days of His flesh, in the way that He says to Aaron and Miriam,
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 609 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son is invisible as God, Word and Spirit, but was visible before the flesh in vision, dream and enigma.
use: answer to objection (the Son is also invisible, so Father and Son are one)
limits: He says the Son is invisible 'in that He is God'. He also says the Son 'was visible before the days of His flesh' in vision and dream, which opponents read as apparent theophany only. The LL bracket placement differs from Kroymann.

latin: non enim et de aliqua maiore persona congruit dicere, Facies mea est ille homo, et, Faciem mihi praestat? Pater, inquit, maior me est: ergo facies erit filii pater. nam et scriptura quid dicit? Spiritus personae eius Christus dominus. ergo si Christus personae paternae spiritus est, merito spiritus cuius persona erat, id est patris eius, faciem suam ex unitate scilicet pronuntiavit. mira res plane an facies filii pater accipi possit qui est caput eius: caput enim Christi deus.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: For is there not a natural propriety in saying of some personage greater (than yourself), That man is my face; he gives me his countenance? My Father, says Christ, is greater than I. John 14:28 Therefore the Father must be the face of the Son. For what does the Scripture say? The Spirit of His person is Christ the Lord. As therefore Christ is the Spirit of the Father's person, there is good reason why, in virtue indeed of the unity, the Spirit of Him to whose person He belonged — that is to say, the Father — pronounced Him to be His face. Now this, to be sure, is an astonishing thing, that the Father can be taken to be the face of the Son, when He is His head; for the head of Christ is God. 1 Corinthians 11:3
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 610 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian uses John 14:28 ('My Father is greater than I') as a reductio: if the greater one is the face of the lesser, the Father would be the face of the Son.
use: objection (John 14:28, 'the Father is greater') answered by a reductio ad absurdum
limits: He gives no reconciliation of John 14:28 here; the argument is a reductio, not an explanation. Arian readers cite John 14:28 for subordination.

latin: sermo enim vitae caro factus, et auditus et visus et contrectatus quia caro, qui ante carnem sermo tantum in primordio apud deum patrem, non pater apud semetipsum. nam etsi deus sermo, sed apud deum, quia ex deo deus, quia cum patre apud patrem.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: Now the Word of life became flesh, and was heard, and was seen, and was handled, because He was flesh who, before He came in the flesh, was the Word in the beginning with God the Father, John 1:1-2 and not the Father with the Word. For although the Word was God, yet was He with God, because He is God of God; and being joined to the Father, is with the Father.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 610 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Word was with God, and because He is God of God He is joined to the Father and is with the Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Word is God, with God, God of God)
limits: 'God of God' (ex deo deus) is a phrase later readers could take as derived divinity. Tertullian does not give a same-substance formula in this passage; that comes in ch. 13.8-9 and ch. 25.1.

latin: Et vidimus gloriam eius tanquam unigeniti a patre, utique filii scilicet visibilis, glorificati a patre invisibili. et ideo, quoniam sermonem dei deum dixerat, ne adiuvaret adversariorum praesumptionem quasi patrem ipsum vidisset, ad distinguendum inter invisibilem patrem et filium visibilem superdicit ex abundanti, Deum nemo vidit unquam.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: And we have seen His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father; John 1:14 that is, of course, (the glory) of the Son, even Him who was visible, and was glorified by the invisible Father. And therefore, inasmuch as he had said that the Word of God was God, in order that he might give no help to the presumption of the adversary, (which pretended) that he had seen the Father Himself and in order to draw a distinction between the invisible Father and the visible Son, he makes the additional assertion, ex abundanti as it were: No man has seen God at any time.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm

what_it_says: Tertullian says the glory John saw was the glory of the visible Son, glorified by the invisible Father, and that 'No man has seen God' means the Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (visible Son, invisible Father)
limits: The English 'the glory of the Son' is ANF's reading of 'filii'. The chapter relies on 1 John 1:1 and John 1:18 for the visible/invisible contrast.

latin: porro si ipse est Christus et pater et filius, quomodo et visus est et invisus? ad hanc diversitatem visi et invisi in unum conferendam qui ex diverso nobis argumentabitur recte utrumque dictum, visibilem quidem in carne, invisibilem vero ante carnem, ut idem sit pater invisibilis ante carnem qui et filius visibilis in carne.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: Now, if Christ is Himself both the Father and the Son, how can He be both the Visible and the Invisible? In order, however, to reconcile this diversity between the Visible and the Invisible, will not some one on the other side argue that the two statements are quite correct: that He was visible indeed in the flesh, but was invisible before His appearance in the flesh; so that He who as the Father was invisible before the flesh, is the same as the Son who was visible in the flesh?
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 610 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)

what_it_says: Tertullian states the Praxean objection that the same Christ cannot be both the visible Son in the flesh and the invisible Father before the flesh.
use: objection (modalist argument, as Tertullian states it); quote only with the answer in ch. 15.4-9
limits: This is the objection, not Tertullian's answer. Quoting it alone would misrepresent him.

latin: ipse enim et ad humana semper colloquia descendit, ab Adam usque ad patriarchas et prophetas, in visione in somnio in speculo in aenigmate ordinem suum praestruens ab initio semper quem erat persecuturus in finem.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: For He it was who at all times came down to hold converse with men, from Adam on to the patriarchs and the prophets, in vision, in dream, in mirror, in dark saying; ever from the beginning laying the foundation of the course of His dispensations, which He meant to follow out to the very last.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 612 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son came down to converse with men from Adam onward in vision, dream, mirror and enigma, rehearsing his future incarnation.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Old Testament theophanies are the Son, the Word)
limits: This is Tertullian's 'rehearsal' theory of theophany; opponents say it makes the Son the visible God of the Old Testament, which is a second deity. Chapter 16.6 also says the one who walked in Paradise was the Son, not the invisible Father; the Latin Library text there has crux-marks around 'et in imagine et speculo et aenigmate'.

latin: Omnia, inquit, patris mea sunt: cur non et nomina? cum ergo legis Deum omnipotentem et Altissimum et Deum virtutum et Regem Israelis et Qui est, vide ne per haec filius etiam demonstretur suo iure Deus <omnipotens> qua sermo Dei omnipotentis quaque omnium accepit potestatem, Altissimus qua dextera dei exaltatus sicut Petrus in Actis contionatur,
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: All things, says He, which the Father has are mine. John 16:15 Then why not His names also? When, therefore, you read of Almighty God, and the Most High, and the God of hosts, and the King of Israel, the One that is, consider whether the Son also be not indicated by these designations, who in His own right is God Almighty, in that He is the Word of Almighty God, and has received power over all; is the Most High, in that He is exalted at the right hand of God, as Peter declares in the Acts;
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm

what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son bears the Father's names (Almighty God, Most High, Lord of hosts, King of Israel, He Who Is) because all things are the Father's and the Son has them.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Son bears the divine names)
limits: The Latin Library gives no heading for ch. 17; the chapter boundary is taken from ANF. The sentence 'the Son is God Almighty ... Word of Almighty God ... received power over all' uses 'Son' and 'power' rather than same-substance language. The Latin Library text has an unreadable character after 'nomen'.

latin: alium autem quomodo dicamus saepe iam edidimus. quo alium dicamus, necesse est non eundem <non eundem> autem non quasi separatum, dispositione alium non divisione.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: But in what sense we call Him Another we have already often described. In that we called Him Another, we must needs imply that He is not identical — not identical indeed, yet not as if separate; Other by dispensation, not by division.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 615 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)

what_it_says: Tertullian says 'Another' (alius) must be understood as distinction by dispensation, not by division, and that the Son is not the same as the one from whom He came.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (distinction without separation)
limits: The phrase 'alius non aliud' does not occur in ch. 13-25 (negative search). The Latin contains editorial '<non eundem>' repeated from the Latin Library apparatus; Kroymann was not checked for this page.

latin: siquidem et legem proponens duorum hominum testimonium confirmantem, subiungit, Ego testimonium dico de me, et testimonium dicit de me qui me misit pater. quodsi unus esset, dum idem est et filius et pater, non citeretur legis patrocinio fidem imponentis non unius testimonio sed duorum.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 34 = PDF p. 64 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-064.png. Kroymann 1907 p.34 reads 'non uteretur legis patrocinio fidem imponentis non unius testimonio, sed duorum' (LL 'non citeretur legis patrocinio'); the rest agrees.
english: Indeed, this was the sum and substance of what He was teaching them, that they were inseparably Two; since, after citing the law when it affirms the truth of two men's testimony, He adds at once: I am one who am bearing witness of myself; and the Father (is another,) who has sent me, and bears witness of me. Now, if He were one — being at once both the Son and the Father — He certainly would not have quoted the sanction of the law, which requires not the testimony of one, but of two.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 617 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian argues from John 8:16-18 that Christ cites the Law's rule of two witnesses, so the one testifying and the Father who sent Him must be two.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (John 8:16-18: two witnesses = two persons)
limits: The argument depends on the legal rule of two witnesses. Kroymann 1907 p.34 reads 'non uteretur legis patrocinio' where LL reads 'non citeretur legis patrocinio'.

latin: si enim dixisset Unus sumus, potuisset adiuvare sententiam illorum:� unus enim singularis numeri significatio videtur. adhuc cum duo masculini generis unum dicit neutrali verbo—quod non pertinet ad singularitatem, sed ad unitatem, ad similitudinem, ad coniunctionem, ad dilectionem patris qui filium diligit, et ad� obsequium filii qui voluntati patris obsequitur—Unum sumus, dicens, ego et pater, ostendit duos esse quos aequat et iungit.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Cross-checked by eye against Kroymann 1907 (Tubingen, Mohr; archive.org tertullianadver00tertgoog), printed p. 36 = PDF p. 66 of the scan, image /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Pruebas/978f574d-1019-54bc-bb45-9f4fddd102bb/scratchpad/tq/T4/dl/kroy_png/p-066.png. Kroymann 1907 p.36 reads 'at nunc, cum duo masculini generis unum dicit neutrali uerbo' (LL 'adhuc cum duo masculini generis unum dicit neutrali verbo'); 'unum sumus', 'non unus sumus', 'duos esse quos aequat et iungit' agree.
english: For if He had said one Person, He might have rendered some assistance to their opinion. Unus, no doubt, indicates the singular number; but (here we have a case where) Two are still the subject in the masculine gender. He accordingly says Unum, a neuter term, which does not imply singularity of number, but unity of essence, likeness, conjunction, affection on the Father's part, who loves the Son, and submission on the Son's, who obeys the Father's will. When He says, I and my Father are one in essence— Unum— He shows that there are Two, whom He puts on an equality and unites in one.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 618 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says 'Unum sumus' (we are one, neuter) signifies unity, not singularity of number, since 'ego et pater' are two persons and the neuter names their unity of likeness, union and love.
use: answer to objection ('I and my Father are one' = one person); Unum (neuter) = unity, not singularity
limits: ANF renders 'Unum' as 'one in essence'; the Latin has only 'unum sumus' and the gloss is the translator's. The Latin lists 'similitudo, coniunctio, dilectio, obsequium' as the content of unity, which opponents may read as moral unity only. Kroymann p.36 reads 'at nunc, cum duo masculini generis' where LL reads 'adhuc cum duo masculini generis'.

latin: quot personae tibi videntur, perversissime Praxea, nisi quot et voces? habes filium in terris, habes patrem in caelis. non est separatio ista, sed dispositio divina.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: how many Persons do you discover, obstinate Praxeas? Are there not as many as there are voices? You have the Son on earth, you have the Father in heaven. Now this is not a separation; it is nothing but the divine dispensation.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 619 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian asks Praxeas how many persons he counts, given that the Son is on earth and the Father in heaven, and says this is a divine dispensation, not a separation.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (distinct persons in the dispensation, not separation)
limits: 'Dispositio' is read by opponents as a mode rather than a person. Tertullian's word here is 'persona' in the sense of a distinct subject.

latin: postulat filius de terris, pater promittit a caelis. quid mendacem facis et patrem et filium? si aut pater de caelis loquebatur ad filium cum ipse esset filius apud terras, aut filius ad patrem precabatur cum ipse esset pater apud caelos, quale est ut filius item postularet a semetipso postulando a patre si filius erat pater, iterum pater sibi ipse promitteret promittendo filio si pater erat? ut sic duos divisos diceremus quomodo iactitatis, tolerabilius erat duos divisos quam unum deum versipellem praedicare.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: The Son offers His request from earth, the Father gives His promise from heaven. Why, then, do you make liars of both the Father and the Son? If either the Father spoke from heaven to the Son when He Himself was the Son on earth, or the Son prayed to the Father when He was Himself the Son in heaven, how happens it that the Son made a request of His own very self, by asking it of the Father, since the Son was the Father? Or, on the other hand, how is it that the Father made a promise to Himself, by making it to the Son, since the Father was the Son? Were we even to maintain that they are two separate gods, as you are so fond of throwing out against us, it would be a more tolerable assertion than the maintenance of so versatile and changeful a God as yours!
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 619 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian answers Praxeas' taunt of 'two gods' by saying two separate gods would be more tolerable than the changeable God Praxeas describes.
use: answer to objection (charge of ditheism)
limits: 'Tolerabilius erat' is rhetorical; opponents quote it as a concession that two gods would be acceptable. It is not a statement of his doctrine.

latin: si ita est, ergo non patrem tanto tempore secum conversatum ignoraverant sed filium: et dominus, eum se ignorati exprobrans quem ignoraverant, eum utique agnosci volebat quem tanto non agnosci tempore exprobraverat, id est filium. et apparere iam potest quomodo dictum sit, Qui me videt videt et patrem: scilicet quo et supra, Ego et pater unum sumus.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: This, then, being the case, it was not the Father whom, after His lengthened intercourse with them, they were ignorant of, but it was the Son; and accordingly the Lord, while upbraiding Philip for not knowing Himself who was the object of their ignorance, wished Himself to be acknowledged indeed as that Being whom He had reproached them for being ignorant of after so long a time — in a word, as the Son. And now it may be seen in what sense it was said, He that has seen me has seen the Father, John 14:9 — even in the same in which it was said in a previous passage, I and my Father are one.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 620 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says that when Christ says 'He that has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9), He is known as the Son, and this is the same sense as 'I and my Father are one' (John 10:30).
use: answer to objection (John 14:9: seeing the Son is seeing the Father)
limits: Tertullian explains John 14:9 by the Son's role as the one known, not by numerical identity. ANF's 'in a word, as the Son' renders the Latin 'id est filium'.

latin: secundum haec enim vicarium se patris ostenderat, per quem pater et videretur in factis et audiretur in verbis et cognosceretur in filio facta et verba patris� administrante: quia invisibilis pater, quod et Philippus didicerat in lege et meminisse debuerat—Deum nemo videbit et vivet.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: For in all these passages He had shown Himself to be the Father's Commissioner, through whose agency even the Father could be seen in His works, and heard in His words, and recognised in the Son's administration of the Father's words and deeds. The Father indeed was invisible, as Philip had learned in the law, and ought at the moment to have remembered: No man shall see God, and live.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 620 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Son was shown as the Father's agent ('vicarium'), through whom the Father is seen in works and heard in words; the Father Himself remains invisible.
use: answer to objection (John 14:9); quote with care, because 'vicarium' is subordinationist wording
limits: Latin 'vicarium' (deputy, agent) is subordinationist wording and is the reason opponents cite this passage. ANF renders it 'Commissioner'. The Latin has an unreadable character after 'patris' (replacement character in the source).

latin: ita connexus patris in filio et filii in paracleto tres efficit cohaerentes alterum ex altero. qui tres unum sunt, non unus, quomodo dictum est, Ego et pater unum sumus, ad substantiae unitatem non ad numeri singularitatem.
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: Thus the connection of the Father in the Son, and of the Son in the Paraclete, produces three coherent Persons, who are yet distinct One from Another. These Three are one essence, not one Person, as it is said, I and my Father are One, John 10:30 in respect of unity of substance not singularity of number.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 621 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Father, Son and Paraclete are three coherent persons who are one thing, not one person, in respect of unity of substance and not singularity of number.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (three persons, one substance)
limits: 'Tres unum sunt' is a neuter claim (one thing, not one person). The English 'one essence' is ANF wording for 'unum' and 'substantiae unitatem'. 'Substantiae unitatem' is his own phrase in this chapter.

latin: Ne, inquit, contigeris me, nondum ascendi ad patrem meum, vade autem ad fratres meos (quin et in hoc filium ostendit, filios enim appellasset illos si pater fuisset) et dices eis, Ascendo ad patrem meum et patrem vestrum, deum meum et deum vestrum. pater ad patrem et deus ad deum? an filius ad patrem et sermo ad deum?
latin_edition: Latin Library, thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praxean.shtml (read verbatim by curl 2026-10-20; the page prints no edition; section marks [n] removed). Not yet checked against Kroymann 1907 for this passage.
english: Jesus says unto her, Touch me not, for I am not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brethren (and even in this He proves Himself to be the Son; for if He had been the Father, He would have called them His children, (instead of His brethren), and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father and your Father, and to my God and your God. John 20:17 Now, does this mean, I ascend as the Father to the Father, and as God to God? Or as the Son to the Father, and as the Word to God?
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. A. Roberts and J. Donaldson); english text read at newadvent.org/fathers/0317.htm
page: ANF vol. 3, p. 621 (Scribner 1918 scan, archive.org antenicenefather03robe; page read from OCR running head, starts on this page; check before print)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Scribner 1918 scan (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03robe) for page numbers; the local PDF is the 'Latin Christianity' vol. 3 scan (archive.org/details/LatinChristianityItsFounderTertullianVol.3OfTheAnte-niceneFathers), whose running head is PDF page + 2
what_it_says: Tertullian asks whether John 20:17 means Father to Father and God to God, or Son to Father and Word to God, and answers the second.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Son and Word distinct from Father and God)
limits: John 20:17 ('my God and your God') is the text Arian readers use for the Son's subordination. Tertullian's answer, 'sermo ad deum', is a rhetorical question, not a formal definition.
